etymology: From traditional + -ism; Latin traditio, a handing over, from tradere, to deliver (trans, across + dare, to give). Not to be confused with traducianism, from tradux, a vine-shoot, which concerns the origin of the soul.
biblical_def: Traditionalism is the habit of holding a thing because it has been handed down, and of treating what the fathers did as binding because the fathers did it. Scripture does not despise tradition. Paul tells the church to “hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and the apostolic deposit is a tradition in the plain sense of the word: a thing delivered. What Scripture condemns is tradition that has come loose from the Word and then been set over it. The Lord’s charge against the Pharisees was not that they kept customs but that they were “making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Peter says his readers were redeemed “from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1 Peter 1:18). So the line runs between two things that look alike. Tradition rightly held is the church’s memory, a servant that hands on what Scripture teaches: the creeds, the confessions, the hymns, the catechism a father teaches his sons. Traditionalism makes the servant a master. It asks first what the church has always done, and only afterward, if at all, what God has said. The 1689 Confession (1.10) names the supreme judge of every controversy as the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit. Councils and ancient writers are examined by that rule. They are never added to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for traditionalism. Under TRADITIONALLY his example sentence is a Protestant one: a doctrine derived by tradition from the apostles is of no authority. Under TRADITIONARY he names the Jewish party that explained the Scriptures by tradition.
webster_full: TRADI’TIONALLY, adv. By transmission from father to son, or from age to age; as an opinion or doctrine traditionally derived from the apostles, is of no authority.

TRADI’TIONARY, n. Among the Jews, one who acknowledges the authority of traditions, and explains the Scriptures by them. The word is used in opposition to Cairite, one who denies the authority of traditions.
scriptures: Mark 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
Mark 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
Colossians 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
2 Thessalonians 2:15
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
1 Peter 1:18
Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
corruption_summary: Traditionalism takes the church’s memory, which exists to serve the Word, and sets it over the Word. Rome made tradition a second source of revelation. The Pharisees made it a fence that broke the law it claimed to guard. A Protestant congregation can do the same thing with nothing more than “we have always done it this way.”
corruption_paragraphs: The formal corruption is Rome’s. The Council of Trent, in its fourth session (1546), received the unwritten traditions with the same affection of piety and reverence as the Scriptures, and made the church’s teaching office the judge of what both mean. That is two sources of revelation and one interpreter who answers to neither. The Reformation did not answer it by throwing tradition away. The Reformers quoted Augustine and the councils constantly. They answered it by putting every tradition under the one rule that God Himself breathed out. That is sola Scriptura: Scripture the only infallible rule, and the church’s confessions honored as subordinate standards beneath it.

The Gospel corruption is the Pharisees’. In Mark 7 the Lord takes the case of Corban. The fifth commandment says a man must honor his father and mother. The tradition of the elders let him declare his goods dedicated to God and so owe his parents nothing. The custom began as a fence around the law and ended as a way out of it. That is the shape every traditionalism takes. It starts by guarding the commandment and finishes by excusing a man from it, and the man who keeps the custom feels more righteous than the man who keeps the commandment.

The historian Jaroslav Pelikan put the difference in one line: “Tradition is the living faith of the dead; traditionalism is the dead faith of the living.” Protestants are not immune. A church can confess sola Scriptura on paper and still settle every question by what the last pastor did, defend an order of service harder than the doctrine it was built to carry, and treat a translation, a hymnal, or a building as untouchable. The Lord sends His people back to “the old paths, where is the good way” (Jeremiah 6:16), and the point is the good way, not the age of the path. Age is evidence that a thing may be worth keeping. It is never proof. The cure is not to despise the fathers but to read them with an open Bible, keep what agrees with it, and drop what does not.
roots_summary: The Greek paradosis means simply “a handing over.” The same word names the apostolic teaching Paul commands the church to hold and the tradition of the elders Christ condemns. What separates them is where the teaching came from and whether it stands under the Word.
roots_lines: Greek paradosis (G3862) — a handing down; tradition, whether apostolic or of men
Greek patroparadotos (G3970) — handed down from the fathers
Latin traditio — a handing over, from tradere, to deliver
usage: Traditionalism asks what the church has always done; faith asks what God has said.
He mistook traditionalism for faithfulness and defended the custom harder than the commandment.
Traditionalism, a view of authority, is not traducianism, a view of the soul’s origin.

etymology: From creation + -ism; Latin creatio, from creare, to make, bring forth. In older theology the word also names the view that God creates each human soul directly (see Creationism of the Soul). In ordinary use it names the belief that God made the world as Genesis records it, against evolutionary naturalism.
biblical_def: Creationism is the confession that the heavens, the earth, and everything in them were made by God, by His word, out of nothing, as Genesis 1–2 records. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The world was not drawn out of matter that was already there, and it was not produced by chance over unguided ages: “the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear” (Hebrews 11:3). The dictionary holds the plain reading of the text: six days of ordinary length, evening and morning, as the Fourth Commandment repeats: “in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is” (Exodus 20:11). Man did not rise from the beasts. God formed Adam from the dust and breathed life into him, then made Eve from his side, and those two are the historical parents of the whole race (Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:22). Christ grounds marriage in that order: “from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female” (Mark 10:6). The 1689 Confession (4.1) says it pleased God to make the world and all things in it in the space of six days, and all very good. Creationism is not first a theory of geology. It is a confession about who owns the world and who owns the man: “thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created” (Revelation 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for creationism. He defines CREATION first as the act of causing to exist, and especially the act of bringing this world into existence, and cites Romans 1:20.
webster_full: CREA’TION, n. 1. The act of creating; the act of causing to exist; and especially, the act of bringing this world into existence. Romans 1:20.
5. The things created; creatures; the world; the universe.
scriptures: Genesis 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Exodus 20:11
For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.
Hebrews 11:3
Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.
Mark 10:6
But from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female.
Romans 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Revelation 4:11
Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.
corruption_summary: The open corruption is evolutionary naturalism, which says the world made itself. The quieter one is theistic evolution, which keeps God’s name on the cover and lets Darwin write the chapters, and which cannot keep Paul’s Adam without rewriting Romans 5.
corruption_paragraphs: Naturalism teaches that matter, time, and chance account for everything, man included. Scripture does not treat that as a neutral finding. Paul says the things that are made show God’s eternal power and Godhead so plainly that men are left “without excuse” (Romans 1:20), and of those who would not glorify Him he says, “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:22). The denial of the Creator is first a moral refusal and only afterward a theory. A man who will not have a Maker will not have a Lawgiver either.

Theistic evolution, sometimes called evolutionary creationism, keeps the Creator and hands the method to Darwin. Genesis 1–11 becomes poetry or myth. Adam becomes a population, or one hominid chosen out of many. Death, disease, and predation become the tools God used for millions of years before any man sinned. That cannot stand with the apostle. “By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Romans 5:12). If death was God’s method of making man, death is not the wages of sin, and the cross answers a problem God built into the world on purpose. Paul’s gospel needs a first Adam: “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Take away the first man and the second Adam has no one to stand for.

Not every departure weighs the same. Some Reformed men, Kuyper and Warfield among them, allowed an older earth while confessing a historical Adam, the fall, and inherited sin. The dictionary does not call that heresy, but it does not take that voice either: Exodus 20:11 ties the week a man works and rests to the week God worked and rested, and the plain reading is the faithful one. The word also has an older theological sense, the view that God creates each human soul directly, which is treated under Creationism of the Soul.
roots_summary: The Hebrew bara’ is the verb of Genesis 1:1, and in its simple form Scripture never gives it any subject but God. Creation is His work alone.
roots_lines: Hebrew bara’ (H1254) — to create; in its simple stem used only of God
usage: Creationism confesses that God made the heavens and the earth in six days and called it very good.
He held to creationism not as a hobby of geology but as the ground of the Sabbath and of marriage.
Creationism, the origin of the world, is distinct from creationism of the soul, the origin of each man’s soul.
